caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Tanzania's debt has nearly tripled as a share of GDP on infrastructure borrowing. From 17.4% in 2006, the series low (post-HIPC), the ratio rose steadily as governments borrowed for railways, ports, and the Julius Nyerere hydropower dam: 49.9% in 2024, the series high, with 49.6% projected for 2025. Borrowing is a mix of concessional and commercial (including Eurobonds), and IMF assessments judge the risk of distress moderate. The pace of the climb is the concern: Tanzania has added over 30 points of GDP in debt in fifteen years, and while growth has kept the ratio manageable, debt service is rising as commercial borrowing grows.
inflation_management: Tanzania's inflation was tamed over the period, falling from 16.0% in 2012, the series high, to 3.1% in 2024, the series low, with 3.3% projected for 2025. The Bank of Tanzania's monetary framework, now moving toward interest-rate-based policy, brought inflation down from double digits in 2008-2012 to the 3-6% range for a decade. The 2022 global shock produced only 4.4%, a testament to the framework's credibility. Food prices remain the main driver, and the central bank has managed the shilling's gradual depreciation without disorder. Tanzania's inflation record is among East Africa's best.

key_events.event: Global food-fuel crisis pushed inflation to 16.0% (2012), the series high.
John Magufuli won the presidency, launching infrastructure megaprojects and resource nationalism.
Magufuli died (March 2021); Samia Suluhu Hassan succeeded him, reopening the economy and diplomacy.
East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP) advanced amid environmental criticism.
Debt reached 49.9% of GDP, the series high, on hydropower and railway borrowing.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued 5-6% growth with inflation near 3-5% and debt stabilizing around 50% of GDP. Upside comes from LNG (if final investment decisions land), EACOP transit fees, and regional trade; downside is that debt keeps climbing toward distress if megaproject spending continues. Uncertainty is moderate: the macro framework is sound and Samia's government is investor-friendly, but the debt trajectory needs to flatten.
